title: Bo: come, not go (Exodus 10:1)
hookLine: God tells Moses "come unto Pharaoh", as if God is already in the room
tomorrow: Bo: darkness that could be felt (Exodus 10:21–23)

lines: GO OUT THERE, OR COME ON.
cards: There's a difference between a coach who says go out there and one who says come on, out we go. Same field, same game. But one of them is staying on the bench, and the other is walking out beside you.
Moses has stood before Pharaoh again and again. Plague after plague, and each time Pharaoh ends up saying no. Moses has every reason to dread going back.
And the portion opens with God sending him back, using a word that, in Hebrew, is a little strange. It isn't the word for go. It's the word for come.

teach.h: BO EL PAR'OH: COME UNTO PHARAOH.
teach.b: The portion is named for that word: Bo. In Hebrew, God says to Moses, bo el Par'oh. The old Jewish translation, like the King James, smooths it into go in unto Pharaoh, and that's fair: the Hebrew verb can mean entering.
But its plain sense is come.
And people who say come are usually already where they're asking you to be. The Zohar, a classic work of Jewish mysticism, plays with exactly this.
It pictures God leading Moses inward, room after room, into the innermost chamber of Pharaoh's power, the place Moses most feared, and saying: come. Not go there alone. Come here, where I already am.
It's a reading, not the plain story, and the Zohar wraps it in a lot of symbolism about the deep places of evil. The simple point doesn't need the symbolism.
Back at the burning bush, Moses had asked who he was to stand before Pharaoh.
God's answer was a short promise: "Certainly I will be with thee." Bo is that promise, folded into one syllable. It doesn't make the room less hard.
The verse even says, right there, that Pharaoh's heart has been hardened. He'll still say no. Moses still has to walk in.
He just doesn't walk in first.

how: Bo is read in synagogues in winter. Some teachers, Hasidic commentators among them, dwell on its first word, reading 'come' as a sign that God goes ahead of Moses into Pharaoh's palace.

o: stand, as when facing a king in his court
come, as when calling someone into a room you're in
go, as when sending someone off on their own

games.q: inside the first verse — tap the pairs.

s: the Hebrew word bo plainly means come
translations often say go in, but the simple sense is come.
after God says come, Pharaoh finally agrees
the same verse says his heart is hardened. the room stays hard.
the room-after-room picture is in the plain text of Exodus
it's the Zohar's reading, a mystical interpretation of the word bo.

games.q: you're Moses. plague after plague, and Pharaoh still says no. God sends you back to Pharaoh. which word does the Hebrew use?
o: come: as if God is already inside.
games.why: bo: come. readers from the Zohar onward hear in it that God is already in the room Moses dreads.

practice: Think of a room you're dreading this week, a meeting, a phone call, a doctor's office, a kitchen where an old argument lives, and picture walking through its door, not as the first one in, but as someone called in by a voice already inside.
If you pray, hold the words I will be with thee as you cross the threshold; if not, picture one person who'd be on your side in there.

wordCard.voice: Bo. Come. The name of this week's portion, and the word God uses to send Moses back to Pharaoh, as if calling him into a room God is already in.

orig.note: Hebrew: come, or enter. the first word God speaks in the portion, and its name.

carryVoice: Your line: come, not go. The room stays hard, but you don't walk in first. Day three hundred thirty-three, done.

sources.q: Certainly I will be with thee.
